endorsements.quote: sponsors should consider the use of dynamic labeling when 1938 possible.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Establish and maintain policies and procedures to record and track GAI system reported errors, near-misses, and negative impacts.

endorsements.title: Could transparent model cards with layered accessible information drive trust and safety in health AI?
endorsements.quote: We advocate for much greater standardization of information supplied to users, with the presentation of this information in highly usable formats, that look the same for every product and use standardized layouts for including, ordering and ranking of information.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether expandable digital formats, visualizations, or user-centered research make model cards and labeling easier for nontechnical users to understand. The recommendation currently rests on one FDA draft guidance that encourages dynamic labeling and one NIST framework whose quoted text addresses error tracking rather than labeling design.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The claim that dense documentation confuses nontechnical users is plausible, but the supplied material does not measure comprehension under any labeling format.

The FDA draft guidance states that sponsors should consider dynamic labeling when possible, which lends partial support to expandable digital formats. The NIST Generative AI Profile passage concerns recording errors, near-misses, and negative impacts, and it does not speak to visualization or audience-centered design. Neither source is binding, since one is draft guidance and the other is a voluntary framework.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare static technical model cards with expandable, visual, or co-designed formats and measure whether clinicians, administrators, and patients correctly identify intended use, performance limits, and known failure conditions. Such studies should also test whether better comprehension changes decisions about when to rely on or override a model.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that labeling designed for a general audience will be understood by their staff or patients, and they would need to conduct their own usability testing.
